utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that one of the parties would like to raise a matter. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's related to -- well, it will be in private session and it is related to the upcoming witness. I understood, though, that there are also something else that the Chamber wished to deal with procedurally before we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I want to deal with a matter procedurally as well. And that's -- you may not be surprised, scheduling for the weeks to come. We could deal with that first, but I do not flow what -- if your matter is related to the next witness, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is related somewhat to the next witness, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first deal with the scheduling. The Chamber has received, Mr. Kay, the schedule for witnesses, which goes until next week, Friday. Now, how realistic is our expectation that we would finish by next Friday? Has there been communication with the other parties so as to know more or less how much time cross-examination would take so as to know whether you could, for example, start with your second expert witness at the time you have on your mind or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're just reviewing the witness list for next week, because there may be one witness who issues have been dealt with through other witnesses. And what I've done as we've gone through this case is reviewed our listed witnesses to see whether -- what challenges there have been, whether issues have been covered, and then taken them off the list if there is no need to call people. I have taken those decisions and I'm reviewing one for next week. That schedule has been put together only from the available information that I've had, as well as a bit of guess-work. My feeling is that the last witness will be into the next week. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means a spillover in the second week of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And just to assist the Court as well, the Court will be reminded we have 92 bis evidence as well to produce in the proceedings as well as the fact that the Rule 68 matter as between the OTP and the Defence is still ongoing and not concluded yet. That is -- that is not problematic because it will be the admitted facts or adjudicated facts that are relied upon, depending upon the sources of evidence. But it's something that eventually will have to come before the Court and be entered on to the record, as well as we'll need a bit of preparation time. The Prosecution and Cermak Defence are in constant communication about this every day as to the best way to handle matters, and I think it's appreciated from the Prosecution side that there is actually more material there that needs to be worked upon and dealt with. We took in mind very much Your Honours' comments about the size of the filing that we made, but we felt we had to make that filing to get something on the table so that at least we were covered that far, and the Court could see our intentions into relation to the evidence to be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we should prepare a Scenario A and Scenario B, the one in which there is some spillover in the second week of November, whereas in the other one we would conclude next week. The reason I'm asking or I'm inquiring is, of course, because usually if there is any delay it should be resolved to some extent by the party who is calling the witness and who is presenting its case at that time. But since we are at the end of the Cermak case means the beginning of the Markac case and therefore -- have you -- there are a few matters of great importance, first to receive, as soon as possible, realistic time estimates for cross-examination of next week's witnesses so that we can see whether -- how realistic it is to expect that you would be able to conclude your case next week. Then, of course, the other matter still outstanding to see whether that all fits within that one week, and, if not, how many days it would, in the week after that. And then, of course, the next question would be whether we would ask the Markac Defence whether they could already start on the Thursday or Friday, or -- or whether they would then prefer to start the week after that. That would be the third week of November. And then, of course, because I'm not only thinking about the few weeks to come but also about third week of November, what would that mean for the scheduling of the Markac Defence on the long-term, that is, the recess period from mid-December until early January. These are matters I -- we will have to consider. And we are asking the co-operation of the parties to give us, as soon as possible, insights on what we could expect to start with for the first two weeks, and then, and I'm looking at you, Mr. Mikulicic, also then to know as soon as possible what we could expect as far as the case presentation for Mr. Markac is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as we're going through matters, it seems to me the spillover into the second week of November, I think, is predictable now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't exclude yet for the possibility that we could still finish next week, but I think I understood your message quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think you understood my message quite well as well. When I said what we need are two scenarios.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one -- the optimistic one, and the other one -- you would say the realistic one, I would say the pessimistic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. In relation to the cross-examination estimates, from our side, the two shorter factual witnesses, Monday, Tuesday, it's one session each. And two experts to follow, it's four to six sessions each. And, of course, I would appreciate if the Cermak Defence would tell us which witnesses or which witness they will drop. I don't know need to repeat that. There is an lot of preparation going on. For instance, for Mr. Mesic, who has been dropped within a week before he was to call. That with a huge witness to prepare. So I'd like to know as soon as I can which witnesses is going to be dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your observations further support the expectation by Mr. Kay because four to six sessions each, average of five, makes -- two times five is ten, which is already more than three full days. Whereas, both for chief and cross, only three days have been scheduled. And I'm not -- have not considered yet any cross-examination by the -- by the other Defence teams. So, therefore, I should perhaps forget about the word pessimistic and talk into terms of realistic. That is clear. Could the Chamber receive -- not necessarily now but also as soon as possible the estimates for cross-examination of both the witnesses of fact and the expert witnesses for next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If they could be sent to us, Your Honour, so that we can put them in our table that we then send to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which gives us a helpful indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would not have expected to leave you out of the list of addressees, Mr. Kay. That was the scheduling issue I wanted to raise. Then we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kay, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. Mr. Cetina, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cetina. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now being handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to take that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Cetina. Mr. Cetina, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, I'd like you to look at the screen on your right and to look at document that comes onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have 2D00726.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a statement that you gave to the Defence, and I would like you to identify it. Can you see there a copy of a witness statement that you gave to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if the Court would kindly move it up a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you identify your signature on that first page?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that a -- a first page of a statement that you gave to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look at the end of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you can see a date on the statement. And you can see a signature. Do you identify that that is the date of a statement? If you can give the date to the Court, because I can't read it from here.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes. The 26th of August, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that your signature at the end of the statement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you confirm that that is a statement that you made to the Defence; and when you signed that statement, did you read through it to check that the information was true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes. I read it, and I confirm the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also sign a supplementary information sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have 2D00776.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, another document will come on the screen, Mr. Cetina, which I'd like you to identify. Do you see there a document dated the 24th of October, 2009? And that's the first page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you turn now to the second page of the statement, please. And the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you identify there your signature with the date of the 26th of October, 2009?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you read through what was written in this supplemental information sheet before you signed that document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is the information contained within this supplemental information sheet, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, they are true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This supplemental information sheet makes certain clarifications and a correction to a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's look at that statement now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And could we have on the screen, please, 2D00725.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you some more questions about this document, Mr. Cetina. That is a copy of your statement to the Office of the Prosecution. Do you confirm that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We notice that on the dates of interview it's recorded that you were interviewed on the 10th and 11th of September, 2001. Are you able to confirm those facts?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we also see that on the 25 and 26th of February, 2002, you were also interviewed on those dates. Are you able to confirm those facts?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, we see on the statement various signatures on the first page. Is your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you confirm that you signed this document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could just now go to the end of that statement, to page -- I think it's 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see there various signatures. Do you identify your signature on that page, on the 26th of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I can't see it here. The document should be moved either to the left or to the right, because I can't see my signature here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There are no other signatures on -- on that page. But your signature's not on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we go to the previous page, one page back?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, here I can see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And if could you just identify which one it is. Is it the one next to where it says -- above the date?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we can just have that as a single page shot now so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now about this OTP interview. First of all, do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were interviewed on the four dates by the Office of the Prosecution, what language did you speak in?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the investigators of the Office of the Prosecution, what language did they speak in?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was there a translator to interpret the English into Croatian and the Croatian into English?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The statement that you signed, was it a statement in your own language, Croatian, or was it a statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I signed it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the statement that you signed, did you read it yourself in Croatian, or did anyone read it to you before you signed it? What was the procedure: Did you read it for yourself or was it read to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I read it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've made certain clarifications and a correction to that statement. Is the information otherwise in that statement to the Office of the Prosecution information that is, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I was to ask you in court today the same questions that caused the answers that were put into the statements, subject to the corrections, would you give the same answers today as the answers that you gave on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, save for the clarifications I made and to which I affixed my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And those have been noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, may I make those three document, starting, first of all, with 2D00726 an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should they be exhibited under one number or preferably under three numbers? Any preference?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we've been giving separate numbers as we've been dealing with matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, could you -- so it would first be the statement given do the Defence as the first one; the second one the supplemental statement given to the Defence; and third one the statement to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter document 2D00726 will be assigned Exhibit D1743. 65 ter number 2D00776 will be assigned Exhibit D1744. 65 ter number 2D00725 will be assigned Exhibit D1745. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, D1743, D1744, D1745 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a couple of matters that needed to be identified within the statement to point out exhibit references. Your Honour, first of all, in page 10 of the statement given to the Office of the Prosecution, there is an document referred to as 0034-1846 to 60, that is D179, an exhibit under seal. I hope that assists Your Honour in cross-referencing these matters. Then, again, at page 10 of the Prosecution statement, there is a document referred to as 0035-7028 to 29. That is Exhibit D808. Also on page 10, there is an document, 0035-6996 to 7. That is Exhibit P271. And now moving to another page, page 8, the third paragraph, 0308-4327 to 28, that is 65 ter number 2806, and I ask that that be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm told it is already come through as an exhibit as P2649. That's happened in the interim, Your Honour. The next reference is at the OTP witness statement, page 12, paragraph 1, is a document 0035-6998 to 7000. That is 2D00727 on the Defence 65 ter list. I ask that that be made an exhibit. There was an application to add this to our 65 ter list. There was no objection by the Prosecution on the 22nd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D1746. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay, if I may interrupt you, at page 8, the third paragraph, the number you read appears on the record a bit different from what I see in the text, but since it is the only number there and since it is already P2649, I think there's no need to read that number again with all the risks of confusion and errors. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm thankful, Your Honour. The next matter is on paragraph 2 of page 12. There's a document referred to as 0035-7076 to 7. That is document 2D00728 on the Defence 65 ter list. There's an application to add that to the 65 ter list with no objection from the Prosecution on the 22nd of September. Your Honour, may this be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D1747. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the last matter, in relation to this, Your Honour, is a document in paragraph 3 of page 12, with the number 0035-7085 to 86. That's on the Prosecution 65 ter list as 974. There's an application to make that an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This becomes Exhibit D1748. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Your Honour. Your Honour, if I may now just give a brief summary of Mr. Cetina's evidence before I ask him some further questions. Mr. Cetina was the chief of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, appointed on the 1st of January, 1995, and the chief during Operation Storm and until the year of 1995 to the end of the year. He knew about Operation Storm about two days before it took place, and he started preparations in relation to the military operation. He was in Zadar when it commenced on the 4th of August, 1995. On the second day of the operation, the 5th of August, 1995, the Ministry of Interior appointed several people to the position of police station commanders, and those appointments were made within the newly created district of Kotar-Knin Police Administration. The chief commander of that police administration was a man called Cedo Romanic, and thereafter various police officers were appointed to the police stations which made up the area of the Kotar-Knin Police Administration. These police administrations were also assisted by coordinators appointed by the Ministry of Interior from Zagreb whose role and responsibility it was was to provide support to the police administrations in taking on these extra tasks caused by the conflict and the occupation of territory that had previously been occupied by the Government of the Republika Srpska Krajina. During his work for Zadar-Knin Police Administration, Mr. Cetina had many meetings with the military police. He had meetings with the UNCIVPOL and other agencies of the UN, and on a few occasions, he met General Cermak to discuss problems within the area. And his evidence is that General Cermak condemned crimes that was happening and wanted to ensure that these problems were stopped. Your Honour, that is a brief summary of the evidence of Mr. Cetina, but I anticipate that further details will become clear during the course of his evidence, so I have not taken too long on this summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, may I ask you, you have told us what the exhibit numbers were of documents shown to the witness on pages 8, 10, three times 12, but on page 9, I find a document, a UN CIVPOL report, where it is unclear to me whether that's already an exhibit or whether you want to tender it into evidence as you did with some of the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is already an exhibit and my apologies for missing it out. It's Exhibit P270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was 0035-6987 up to and including last two digits 88 being P270. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Cetina, having concluded those formalities, I will now ask you some questions. The first matter I want to deal with concerns the situation before Operation Oluja. At that time, as of the 1st of January, 1995, you were the chief of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Operation Oluja happened on the 4th of August, 1995, and was successfully concluded on the 5th of August, 1995, and we know from your evidence that the Kotar-Knin Police Administration was formed on the 5th of August, with Cedo Romanic as its chief; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's concerning the preparations for the Kotar-Knin Police Administration that I now want to question you about. Was the territory of the Kotar-Knin Police Administration the territory that was previously occupied by the RSK?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was any part of your territory, of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, also occupied by the RSK?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So from the 5th of August, you, for the first time, had jurisdiction over your entire area of responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to your police administration territorial area, did you have to open any new police stations that were subject to the Zadar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And which police stations were they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: They were police stations in Korenica, Obrovac, Donji Lapac, Benkovac, Knin, Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Cedo Romanic was appointed the chief of the Kotar-Knin Police Administration on the 5th of August, 1995. Had there been any preparations made prior to that date for someone to be appointed to the position of chief of that police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: He was appointed by the ministry at its head office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had any preparations been made before that date - so in June or July or earlier months - to prepare him or anyone for that task?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The new police stations that were also opened had police commanders in charge of them. Had any of them been prepared prior to the liberation of the territory for taking on these positions in advance?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to equipment for the police buildings at the police stations, as well as in the Kotar-Knin Police Administration, had there been any advance preparation or storage of equipment, such as computers, office machinery, police equipment? Anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had any of the police officers been identified in advance as to who would be taking on positions within the police stations eventually? Any of those police officers who worked there eventually, had any of them been prepared or identified in advance with the work that they would eventually be doing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to particular areas of police work, such as criminal police investigation, technical equipment, had any of those police stations or the Kotar-Knin Police Administration been provided in advance with technical scientific equipment for police work?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Prior to Operation Storm, were you at a meeting chaired by Mr. Moric, the assistant minister in the Ministry of Interior, on the 3rd of August? So the day before Operation Storm when preparations were made for what was to happen.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were those preparations in respect of the police role during the actual operation itself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: We were given general information to the effect that Operation Storm would commence and that we should be prepared for it. There were no specific preparations made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And perhaps if -- if you could describe the sort of preparations, if any, that you took. What did you do as a result of that meeting on the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I returned to Zadar where I gathered the members of my specialist team. I informed them of the imminent operation and told them that we should get prepared for the return to that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any planning that was done in advance for the situation of check-points or areas of patrol?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No. Our primary objective was to reach the location and to get settled in the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any information or knowledge in advance as to what you might find when you got into the police station?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any training or outlines done as to the kinds of tasks that that police station would have to do when it started functioning?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, we referred to the rules of procedure that were generally in place. And the law governing the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, in relation to coordinators who were appointed by the Ministry of Interior, when were they appointed to assist the police administrations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Very soon, after the beginning of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What exactly was the relationship between the Zadar-Knin Police Administration and the Kotar-Knin Police Administration? Could you describe how they existed together? Was the Zadar-Knin Police Administration superior to Kotar-Knin? Could you describe for us the relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: At the beginning, in a way, yes, it was superior. However, the Kotar-Knin Police Administration, -- or, rather, its chief, could communicate with the ministry directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know from evidence in this court that on 6th of August, Minister Jarnjak came down and opened the police station officially in Knin. Were you present when that happened?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we've heard him on a TV transcript welcoming the new chief, in relation to his work. From -- from that moment, was Cedo Romanic the man in charge of the police administration in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how many police officers he would have had under his command when that police station was opened on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: About 100, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And those police officers were coming into a new police administration. Are you able to tell us where they came from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: They came from all over Croatia, since we didn't have enough men to cover the area ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the types of police officers that were within the Kotar-Knin Police Administration from that day, where were they drawn from? What types of officers were they? Ordinary police, or were they investigators, or administration? What type of police people were they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: They were the so-called ordinary or uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the start, did Kotar-Knin Police Administration have a criminal investigation service, its own?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to criminal investigation service, where would the Kotar-Knin Police Administration have obtained that service? Which -- where would they have got it from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: The Zadar-Knin Police Administration had a crime department within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, just as part of background, how many police officers were within your police administration overall, are you able to tell us that, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, before it entered this territory, there were about 500. And afterwards, another 500, which makes it a thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so we have the picture. How many of those officers were involved in the criminal investigation service?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: About 40 to 50. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, was that number of police in the criminal investigation service increased within your police administration, or did it remain the same?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: It remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, for matters such as recording crimes and detailing what steps had to be taken in relation to crimes, how did the Kotar-Knin Police Administration operate? How did it deal with such matters?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: They would take note of the event that had happened, provide security for the site, and assess whether they needed to call in the criminal police or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, were the numbers of the police available to the Kotar-Knin Police Administration increased from that initial 100?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, in terms of kilometres, first of all, what size of area your police administration, when it occupied all its territory, covered? How big was it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: It was the largest police administration in the country at the time, in terms of territory, but I really can't tell you how many kilometre it covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, after Operation Storm, is it correct that the minister of the interior sent down various senior officers to assist both you, as well as Mr. Romanic, in the Kotar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One, in particular, I want to ask you questions about is Mr. Djurica. Was he an assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: He was -- well, he wasn't the assistant minister. He was the chief of the police sector of the uniformed police in the ministry. And he was the principal coordinator for the Kotar-Knin Police Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he provide assistance to both you and Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have enough police to deal with the problems after Operation Storm within your police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Romanic, at the Kotar-Knin Police Administration, did he have enough police to deal with the problems after Operation Storm in his police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you explain that to Mr. Djurica or any other senior figure from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was the reaction from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, they mostly said that they would help and that they would increase the number of personnel, vehicles, and resources generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did that happen? Were the numbers of personnel sufficiently increased to help you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what about equipment, such as vehicles? Were -- were enough vehicles to patrol provided to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, they were modest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the scale of the problem that was faced after Operation Storm adequately planned for by the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No. Because the situation could not have been foreseen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you now some -- some other questions, and that concerns your contact with the military police. Prior to Operation Storm, did you have contact as the chief of the police administration with the Croatian military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could have a look at a -- a document, P493. And on this right-hand screen again, Mr. Cetina, you'll see a document coming up. It's dated the 3rd of August, 1995. It's from the Ministry of the Interior, and it's sent to the police administrations, including Zadar-Knin. And it concerns co-operation with military police. And it says: "In accordance with the agreed procedure in relation to representatives of the Ministry of Defence, military police, in order to ensure coordinated and harmonised joint action in the newly liberated part of the Republic of Croatia ..." An order is issued that you were to establish contacts with the military police units within the police administration and agree on harmonised action in the implementation of tasks? First of all, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take any steps in relation to this order which was from Mr. Moric, the assistant minister, as of the 3rd of August, before Operation Storm, did you establish contact with the military police units in your area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: It was the chiefs of the departments that were subordinated to me who would have done things like that. They were initial contacts, the first steps, without any meetings having taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if could you just explain how you organised your Zadar-Knin Police Administration. You were the chief. How you organised then these contacts within point 1 with the military police. Who were your subordinates who contacted the military police, at what level, what did they do? If you could just explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: It was the chief the police department, the uniformed police, that is, Mr. Bitanga was his name, and he contacted the military police in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And which military police was -- was that? If you could identify them, what the unit was.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the 71st and 72nd Battalion, and they were headquartered in Rijeka and Split, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So how did you deal with this with Mr. Bitanga? What did you -- did you explain anything to him, how did you get him to implement this order from Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, he knew the commanders beforehand, and so they would get in touch and agree on further co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn now to document D1283.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Another document, Mr. Cetina. It's dated the 4th of August, 1995. It's from the 72nd Military Police Battalion, 3rd Company, Zadar. It's a report to commander. And you can see that it says that a meeting was held on the 3rd of August on the premises of the 72nd Military Police Battalion with a Major Ivan Juric. And -- who issued certain orders in connection with the Croatian military activities. And we see in the second paragraphs that contact was established, including with the chiefs of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration. And this document is from a Captain Viktor Grancaric. First of all, do you know Commander Grancaric, of the 3rd Company in Zadar of the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No. He wasn't at that level of command. He was at the level of command of Chief Bitanga.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the meeting that's referred to here, when it says "chiefs of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration," would that have been, then, Mr. Bitanga's level below you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we just go to the second page of the document in the English, we'll see a list of places. Can you see there some various place names. And it says: two military policemen, two employees of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, establish check-points with the military police. Was that the decision that Mr. Bitanga would have taken, in operation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, he could have made a decision like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just go to another document, 65 ter 2310.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a report from Mr. Grancaric, Captain Grancaric, of the 72nd Military Police, 3rd Company, Zadar, it's dated the 10th of August, 1995. And it refers to -- in the report from the 3rd till 9th of August, and it says in the first sentence: "After meetings with the coordinator of the military police, Major Ivan Juric, the head of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, commander of the operation group, Colonel Mladen Fuzul, head of SIS. And it goes on to refer to issuing tasks. It's just this matter here I wanted to ask you about, where -- first of all, Major Juric, did you ever meet a coordinator for the military police from the military police administration, Major Ivan Juric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Possibly once, but I don't really remember. He might have been at Plitvice, that meeting that was held there later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Where it refers to the head of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration and goes on to refer to Colonel Fuzul, would that have been you identified there in this report?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I think this is wrong. I think that was the chief from the Knin administration. I don't remember having attended that meeting myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to turn now to another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's -- can I make that an exhibit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's first deal with that then. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1749. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1749 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock. It's a bit earlier, but since you're moving to another document, we'll have to take the break rather strict at 3.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's take it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that, may I just -- so that the -- it's line -- page 30, line 19 there is a correction. It's just the way the name is written Major Juric is written with D-j-u-r-i-c. I believe it should be J-u-r-i-c, being sure that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you know that usually the transcript is reviewed after the court hearings. If you have any such technical remark, the best of dealing with it is to write it down on a piece of paper and give it to the transcriber so that it's, for certain, that it appears appropriate. But, nevertheless, thanks for your accuracy, Ms. Mahindaratne. We will have a -- no, let me first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We will have a break, Mr. Cetina, and we would like to see you back in approximately 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We talked about scheduling for next week. The Chamber has received the time estimates for this witness, and it seems that, if everyone behaves very disciplined, that there would be a fair possibility to conclude the evidence of this witness on Friday, so that he doesn't have to stay over the weekend. The parties are urged and encouraged to -- not only to stick to their time-limits - we lost in the beginning some time on procedural matters - but also, if possible, to leave some time for Chamber's questions as well. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have Exhibit D46, please. Letter from Mr. Moric to General Lausic of the military police administration on the 10th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you look at this letter, please, Mr. Cetina. Mr. Moric writes: "According to reports from the field, and in particular the territories of Lika-Senj and Zadar-Knin Police Administrations and Vojnic and Vrginmost areas, cases are being noted of individual Croatian army members on liberated territory stealing movable property and burning houses and killing the cattle that strays around the area." And it refers to a lack of co-operation at check-points and roadblocks between the MUP police and military police members. First of all, what had you communicated to Mr. Moric about what was happening in the field?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: According to the vertical chain of command, we sent daily reports on the events we noted in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were these day reports summaries of what your police stations were receiving as reports?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes. These were collated reports that were sent on a daily basis to the headquarters of the ministry, and all the police administrations affected by Operation Storm had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just so that we now how the system worked, did individual police stations report to your police administration and then did you send the information to Zagreb, having collected it together?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Precisely so. Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can look at D49 next, Exhibit D49, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This also comes from Mr. Moric. It's dated the 18th of August and goes to your police administration as well as to the Knin police station. And we see there, again, the paragraph: "Written and oral reports by police stations and police administrations shows [sic] that there are daily cases of torching houses and illegal taking away of people's movable property in areas liberated in Operation Storm." And then it refers to individuals wearing Croatian army uniforms. And it goes into an order. And it's that I want to look at. Point 1 of the order says: "Police administration chiefs must immediately convene a meeting with commanders of military police battalions to inform them of the problem and of the decision to put a stop to it ..." Did you convene a meeting with the commanders of the military police battalions in your police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I passed the order from the ministry down to the chief of the uniformed police department, Mr. Bitanga.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you give Mr. Bitanga any instructions as to what to do?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: The order is quite clear and self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So is it a -- did you give him a copy of this order?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: The competent chief would receive every single order which came from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it only Mr. Bitanga that you gave this to, or was there any other of your chiefs within your police administration whom you also passed it on to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: It is highly likely that we gave it to the Kotar-Knin Police Administration and to the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In point 2, Mr. Moric requires that: "The meeting must be informed of the decision that cases of torching of houses and ... taking of ... property ... will not be operatively investigated, but a stop must be put to cases of this type as of today ..." Are you able to explain what that meant to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what Mr. Moric meant by it. However, by that date, we had already processed a certain number of cases and had already confiscated the property that had been appropriated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did this part of the order have any effect on how you conducted your police operations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No. To the best of our abilities, we had already been abiding by and implementing the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In point 3, it says: "... commanders of military police battalions are to be requested that mixed barrier check-points and mixed patrols of civilian and military police be set up in all populated areas where there are members of the Croatian army ... and the check-points and patrols will ... prevent the ... problems." Did you have, at that time, a system of joint check-points and joint patrols with the military police within your police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: We had always set up the necessary check-points independently. It was difficult to come to an agreement with the military police because their forces were far weaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to give a figure as to how many military police officers there were within your police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know the figures. Fewer, at any -- by all means, fewer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what about in Kotar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: The same applied to that -- to that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, may I seek a clarification of one of the previous answers. Mr. Cetina, Mr. Kay asked you whether the -- whether the part of the order where it said that it should be stopped, stealing and such kind of things, you said that it had no effect and how you conducted your police stations because, to the best of your abilities, you already been abiding and implementing the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Code. In your previous answer, you said that you had already processed a certain number of cases and had already confiscated the property that had been appropriated. Now, it's not entirely clear to me what you meant by "we had already been abiding and implementing the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Criminal Code." Would that mean that you would continue any investigation that had started already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the early days, as far as we were able to, in every case where a person was stopped in a vehicle with misappropriated goods, we took the proper course of action. In that context, the order issued by Mr. Moric did not add anything new to our activity, did not mean anything specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you be concrete. If there was car, you found a car with misappropriated goods, you took the proper course of action. What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that the vehicle and the goods, if they were stolen, were confiscated and a criminal report was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you would receive a report from someone who said, Well, last week this and this happened; I was -- my property was stolen, would you then further investigate that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was the required degree of suspicion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you just ignored the order that torching of houses and taking of property should not be operatively investigated. You ignored that order? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. We were acting in accordance with the Law on the Interior and the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever respond to that order in a way that you would not obey to it but that you would do what you were supposed to do under the legislation which was effective at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need for such a response, because the laws that I referred to had supremacy over the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And dealing with one matter arising from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you say the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Law on Internal Affairs, rather than the Criminal Code? It was translated as the Criminal Code, but did you say Law on Internal Affairs? Page 35, line 7.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I said the Law on Internal Affairs and the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And it's the Law on Internal Affairs that requires you to act as soon as you have information concerning a crime?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more question in this respect. Mr. Cetina, do I understand your testimony well that you say that this order actually is in violation of the law was in effect at the time? Because it orders you to do something which you say, We couldn't do that because the law tells us to do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whenever the law envisaged such a course of procedure, that was the way we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not my question. My question was whether you then considered this order to be in violation of the existing legislation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a certain way, it is not, in fact, in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, in a certain way, it's a violation of the law. That's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to Exhibit D584, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document from you, Mr. Cetina, dated the 19th of August, 1995. And it concerns the document we've just been looking at from Mr. Moric. And it says: "Please be informed that we had a meeting on the 16th of August, 1995 with the Deputy Commander of the 72nd Battalion of the military police, Mr. Primorac, and on the 17th of August, 1995, with the commander of the 71st Battalion of the military police, Mr. Matanic, during which the tasks from your telegram ... were elaborated. Please note that the Deputy Commander and the Commander of the military police pointed out that coordinated action at all check-points was impossible due to the lack of personnel." Firstly, was that a meeting that you personally had, or was it, again, Mr. Bitanga?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think it was Mr. Bitanga who chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did he report this to you about the military police having lack of personnel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go to Exhibit D1071.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is from the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Major Budimir, dated the 19th of August, 1995, and it goes to the chief of the military police administration, General Lausic. And it concerns a similar order to Mr. Moric's that Mr. Lausic had made concerning co-operation. And it's his report to him. We can see in paragraph 1: Coordination meeting with Mr. Radalj, head of police sector in Split-Dalmatia. Do you know Mr. Radalj of the Split-Dalmatia Police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was his position the equivalent of Mr. Bitanga's?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In Sinj we can see coordination meeting with Mr. Bilobrk. And in number 3, Sibenik, again, a coordination meeting. We can see about the matters raised there. And then in number 4, it says a coordinating meeting was not held in Zadar-Knin Police Administration, because, according to Mr. Cetina, head of the police administration, he orders to establish contact at the level of command of the military police battalion, 71 and 72, and no orders on establishing contact at lower levels. Also, he said he would organise a meeting at the level of commands of these two military police battalions, which carry out military and police tasks in the territory of the police administration. Do you have a comment to make on that point made by Commander Budimir concerning your contact with the command of the 71st and the 72nd?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: This is precisely what I said a moment ago. In other words, that it was Chief Bitanga who was supposed to make that contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I now turn to Exhibit D50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is another order from Mr. Moric to the police administrations on the 22nd of August, 1995, and concerns that order we saw on the 18th of August. And he sets out his order of the linking with the military police to stop houses being burnt, property being taken. The letter sent to the military police administration describing the issue and what the military police administration had asked the battalions to do. And then he asked for the problem at the state level to be monitored, and he was to be informed by reports about co-operation with the military police, and it's sent out, 1, 2, 3, and 4, the types of co-operation and information that he wanted. And in 5, 6, 7, and in the next page in the English, statistics concerning investigations, crimes, and how many perpetrators were wearing Croatian military uniform and how many have abused the uniform, and with a date for the reports. Did you take steps, as a result of receiving this order, to monitor these matters?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go to another document, at Exhibit D586.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is from Mr. Moric to General Lausic of the military police administration. And it, again, discusses further the issue that we have been looking at. And we can see in the second paragraph that information had been received about the demobilisation of a certain number of conscripts has begun and more extensive -- probably meaning demobilisation can be expected, and then describing what problems could be happening. And he makes proposals in relation to dealing with this problem. If I can ask you this: Demobilisation of troops from the Croatian army after the liberation of the occupied territories, did that have an effect upon crime within your police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I presume so. These individuals hailed from the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to describe what happened, then, in relation to conscripts being demobilised? What effect did that have within your police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I believe to this day that these were individuals who had probably kept or held on to quite an amount of weapons and to their uniforms, that they were the ones who committed the crimes that were the subject of our reports to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just looking at this document, there are problems mentioned within this document that there are still no foot patrols due to lack of military policemen who still cannot join up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that something you were aware of, Mr. Cetina, about the shortage of military police for patrols within Kotar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in the fourth paragraph, it refers to during joint meetings we've learned that members of the military police at command are located at the outermost boundaries of our security zone. And it mentions Dabar and a number of other places which are beyond my linguistic skills, but I'll pick out the ones I can pronounce: Drnis, Otric, Mostine, Vrlika-Kijevo, et cetera. We can see the places there. Are you able to comment on that particular problem of military police being at the outermost boundaries of the territory of the Kotar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: All I can say is that they did not stick to the agreement reached with us. Now, the reason why they were up at those positions, I really don't know what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know anything about those places listed in this document, whether they had any significance in relation to the -- what the military was doing and the needs of the military police to be in those places?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The coordination between the Kotar-Knin Police Administration and the 72nd Military Police Battalion, was that something you knew about at the time? Did you discuss that with Mr. Romanic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, I did discuss it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what did he describe his co-operation as being with the 72nd? What type of co-operation did he have?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: He didn't have proper co-operation, and, in fact, we had agreed that he should report directly about that, report to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And he had the right and duty to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go to Exhibit P498.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a report from you to Mr. Moric on the 24th of August concerning your co-operation. And we can see in the second paragraph that you say: "The co-operation between police administrations, police stations, and branch ... stations is ... satisfactory." You don't have major complaints. There are still some cases of house burning, destruction of houses, removal of property, but to a lesser extent than was the case before the 18th of August. The perpetrators of these acts are, for the most part, persons in Croatian army uniforms, civilians, and there are also a few cases of police personnel who appear in uniform. The phrase "of persons in Croatian army uniforms," what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: If we weren't able to identify the persons or, rather, the individuals who had insignia of the Croatian army, then this is how we would describe them, or refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So could civilians wearing Croatian army uniforms with insignia fall into that category of persons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: If we were able to establish their identity, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It says here further on that: "The military police is to a maximum degree involved in criminal investigation. They deal with uniformed persons while other cases are dealt with by civilian police personnel." Could you say what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is this. Once it was established that an individual was officially a member of the Croatian army, then it was our duty, and we insisted upon, having the crime police of the military police be included in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know how many crime police of the military police were in -- were within your territorial area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look down here at the -- at cases "and following an investigation, 15 civilian perpetrators, four in civilian police uniforms identified, we don't have exact information about members of the HV since they are being handled by the military police ..." Did you keep any figures on the numbers of HV personnel that were handed over to the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I don't remember keeping that kind of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go to Exhibit D589.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a report by you dated the 28th of August. Again, to Mr. Moric on the same matter. It concerns treatment of persons in military uniforms. It says: "During the past several days, a significant number of persons wearing Croatian army uniforms, carrying long and short-barrelled arms, driving in cars and other vehicles with civilian registration plates have been observed on patrols ..." Now, that piece of information there, about "persons wearing Croatian army uniforms being in cars and other vehicles with civilian registration plates," what type of people were they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I'd like to see the lower half of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I can't see who signed it. Yes, it was signed by Mr. Marijan Tomurad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Tomurad, his position was what, within the Zadar-Knin Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: He was the deputy. He replaced Mr. Djurica as main coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. So that piece of information there about persons wearing Croatian army uniforms but being in cars and other vehicles with civilian registration plates, were those serving HV soldiers, or were there any other type of other person?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I -- there is one, I think, important -- actually, two words -- a phrase that was omitted from the question. If the -- if Mr. Registrar could take the document to the -- to the previous page, the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could -- if could you just draw the attention of Mr. Kay to where --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can deal with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kay is aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, I can see -- thank you. It says significant number of persons wearing HV Croatian army uniforms of various units carrying long and short-barrelled arms, driving in cars and other vehicles with civilian registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Cetina, is: Who were these people? Are they able to be identified?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: This document was signed by Mr. Tomurad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able do comment on -- on what he was observing there and writing in this report to Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can comment. It was probably on the basis of the information that he had, whether gained personally or information received from others, other police chiefs, that this was a problem that they were facing. That is to say that persons wearing uniforms were moving around, bearing weapons, and moving around in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Further on in this report, in the last paragraph, it says: "I also deem it necessary to achieve an agreement according do which the chief of the Zadar-Knin Police Administration, or the Knin district police administration, or persons authorised by them, may be present at the meetings that General Cermak holds with members of the UNCRO, UNCIVPOL, and other international organisations in Knin, so as to ensure that the police are informed about all agreements and conclusions reached which will enable them to organise and plan tasks and duties from their purview, accordingly." Are you able to explain to what this refers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: This was a good proposal on the part of Mr. Tomurad. And the police was very much interested in receiving all manner of information about crimes and, by the same token, information from UNCRO and UNCIVPOL. And since we knew that Mr. Cermak was holding meetings, he did not have any authorisation to manage police procedure. We thought that it was necessary for one of us to be there and to take over the information from members of UNCRO and UNCIVPOL. And that was the sole motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that whilst Mr. Moric was making these orders to the police administrations on co-operation and coordination that, in a parallel way, General Lausic was also making similar orders of co-operation and coordination to the Military Police Battalions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President, leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, the question was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, yes. I don't particularly see any problem arising from it. I mean, I think sometimes evidence is to be taken in a reasonable way. I'm asking if he was aware of any reports from General Lausic to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there was more in your question, Mr. Kay. But if you would rephrase it, then -- it's -- and, at the same time, Ms. Mahindaratne is reminded that objecting on the basis of leading should be limited to where it really makes a difference. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, shall we look at a document, then, Exhibit D1072.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's dated the 30th of August from General Lausic of the military police administration to the military police battalions. Its subject is coordination meetings with members of the MUP regarding more effective co-operation. And in this report -- this order, he requires daily exchange of daily reports. Were you aware of steps being taken by General Lausic in which he was making these kinds of orders to his military police battalions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before. But I assumed, that - just like Mr. Moric - this was sent to, or certainly orders were sent out to, in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we now turn to Exhibit P499.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're awaiting for it to appear, you earlier quoted, Mr. Kay, from P498. And that was about the 15 civilians and where the document says "and four in civilian police uniform," it's now as a comma which could give it quite a different meaning. So, therefore, could I insist on very precise quoting. You know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says 15 -- if you say comma four it could be understood as "four of which," whereas if it's a "and four" then that has a different meaning and that's the reason why I'm -- it's not very vital for your question because your question finally resulted in something else, but I'd rather have that as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't think I mentioned "comma," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't mention "comma," but you did not read "and," from what I remember, and that has caused it to appear in the transcript as "comma."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. P499 is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it should not be shown to the public, and I take it then that you'll consider the confidential character of the document in your questioning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 1st of September, 1995, from the Kotar-Knin Police Administration and sent to Mr. Moric in Zagreb, further to those orders of his for reports. And it says: "Please be informed we had holding joint meetings can the commanders of the 72nd Battalion of the military police in the area covered by the Knin district police administration. Military police personnel have not been included in the joint work at check-points. They act only on their own orders. The last line of the security zone: "Coordination and joint co-operation are inadequate. The commanders are unable to allocate the necessary number of personnel to have a permanent physical presence at check-points, and they only agree to act on our reports when the perpetrators are members of the Croatian army, who they also deal with at our request." But this problem here, within the Kotar-Knin Police Administration concerning the number of military police, was that something that you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Yes, in a way, yes. Well, that means that if an agreement had been reached at a higher level, then, on the ground, they either acted as best they could or had a shortage of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what was your expectation as between the co-operation being ordered by Mr. Moric, as well as the co-operation being ordered by the military police administration, General Lausic? What was your expectation from the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA CETINA
utterances.text: Well, the expectations were that they should -- we should man the check-points jointly. That is to say, to have the necessary number of men, the number that we had agreed upon, and to implement that. However, in practice, that happened very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could go to 2D00783. Your Honour, may I have leave to add this to the Rule 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a document signed for you by Mr. Kardum dated the 1st of September, and it's sent to all police stations with a deadline for commanders. And this document goes to Kotar-Knin Police Administration, Gambiroza Zvonko, every commander is to deliver a report on these tasks. And then we see: "For the purpose of stopping houses been burnt and other people's removal property being taken away ... it is being ordered to link the VP with the PU and PPs in order to solve this problem." And then: "In order to monitor the problem at the police administration level ..." These points are set out concerning co-operation and statistics. And then a written report was required to be sent to the deputy chief of the basic crime police section at Zadar-Knin Police Administration?
